abstract:
BMD006 is an off-the-shelf antitumor mRNA vaccine targeting lung cancer and lung metastatic solid tumors.

This is a single-center, open-label, dose-escalation clinical trial. The study aims to evaluate the safety, tolerability, preliminary efficacy, pharmacokinetic (PK), and pharmacodynamic (PD) profiles of BMD006 in patients with advanced lung cancer or advanced solid tumors with lung metastasis who have progressed on or are ineligible for standard therapeutic options. This trial also further explores the clinical efficacy of BMD006 in combination with Immuno-Oncology (IO) therapy.

This first-in-human, dose-escalation Phase 1 trial evaluates the safety, tolerability, and immunogenicity of VXCO-102 in healthy young adults across multiple sites in Australia.

All participants will undergo ongoing safety monitoring and immune response assessments through clinical evaluations, sample collection, and participant reporting.

abstract: Despite the remarkable clinical success of immunotherapy, its efficacy against hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains severely limited, highlighting an urgent need for novel targets and strategies to overcome immune evasion. Here, we aimed to identify key regulators of HCC immunity via unbiased functional screening and develop a targeted therapy to remodel the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). We performed an in vivo CRISPR-knockout screen using a 4500-gene sgRNA library in syngeneic HCC mouse models. Single-cell RNA sequencing of human HCC tissues and in vivo macrophage-depletion assays were utilized to dissect cellular populations and validate underlying mechanisms. We identified ribosomal protein S19 (RPS19) as a central mediator of HCC immune evasion, whose deletion in HCC cells mitigates the immunosuppressive TME. Mechanistically, scRNA-seq pinpointed tumor-associated macrophages as the key effector subset, whereby complement C5a receptor 1 (C5aR1) transduces RPS19 signals to trigger macrophage-dependent immune suppression. We further constructed SP94-peptide-modified disulfide-bond-containing nanoparticles (SNPSS) for targeted CRISPR-Cas9 delivery. SNPSS efficiently homes to HCC cells, releases payloads within the glutathione-rich TME, downregulates RPS19, reverses immune suppression, and robustly suppresses HCC progression in vivo. Collectively, the RPS19-C5aR1-macrophage axis fuels HCC immune escape, and SNPSS-based RPS19 gene-editing offers a promising strategy to remodel the TME and boost HCC immunotherapy efficacy.

abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor-natural killer (CAR-NK) cells combine innate cytotoxicity with antigen-directed killing and promise as an immunotherapy with lower cytokine toxicity than CAR-T approaches. However, clinical translation is limited by challenges in transduction, persistence, tumor infiltration, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). We performed a comprehensive literature review of recent preclinical and early-phase clinical studies, engineering strategies (CAR design, transduction technologies, gene-editing), manufacturing and expansion protocols, and trial outcomes in this review. We noted a reference to the advantages of CAR-NK, like multimodal killing (CAR-dependent and innate pathways), potential for allogeneic "off-the-shelf" use, and favorable early safety profiles. However, NK-specific obstacles persist: lower viral transduction efficiencies, short in vivo persistence, poor infiltration into solid tumors, and TME-mediated suppression (TGF-β, adenosine, metabolic stress). Engineering countermeasures such as IL-15 expression, checkpoint receptor knockout, chemokine receptor co-expression (e.g., CXCR1/4), DAP10/DAP12-based signaling domains, and non-viral delivery (transposons/CRISPR) have shown preclinical promise. CAR-NK therapy has developed from concept to a clinically actionable treatment line for hematologic malignancies and shows emerging potential in solid tumors when combined with TME-modulating strategies. This review provides robust evidence about CAR-NK therapies in hematological and solid tumors, with a great emphasis on the challenges they encounter, strategies, and innovative approaches to overcome these challenges, and forward-looking perspectives to improve future therapeutic CAR-NK designs and clinical outcomes.

abstract: Precise, reversible control of transgene expression is essential for safe and durable gene therapy, yet current inducible systems remain difficult to translate in vivo due to large size, limited induction duration, and dependence on immunogenic regulators. Here, we present the adaptamer (adenosine deaminases acting on RNA [ADAR]-modulatable aptamer), a compact (<120 base pair) RNA switch that couples FDA-approved small-molecule-responsive aptamers with endogenous ADAR-mediated RNA editing to regulate expression. Ligand binding stabilizes a double-stranded RNA structure that recruits ADAR to convert a stop codon into a sense codon, restoring downstream protein translation. This cleavage-free, post-transcriptional mechanism enables precise, small-molecule-dependent modulation without exogenous protein machinery. We demonstrate that adaptamers are highly functional across multiple cell lines, including human T cells. In mice, adeno-associated virus (AAV)-delivered adaptamer-controlled FGF21 expression induced metabolic remodeling, reversing obesity and hepatic steatosis. This minimal, programmable system offers a clinically compatible approach for tunable genetic medicines and safe deployment of pleiotropic and dose-limited proteins.

abstract: Advanced therapeutics, including programmable nucleic acid-based therapies (NATs), such as small interfering RNAs (siRNAs), antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), CRISPR-Cas 9 editing systems, modified in vitro transcribed messenger RNAs (mRNAs) and Adeno-associated viruses (AAVs), have the potential to transform healthcare. However, while there have been considerable successes, there have also been notable clinical failures in early-stage human trials, which slowed down the progression of these therapeutic platforms. Multiple trials of NATs have been halted or discontinued, or approved products carry black box warnings as unforeseen or underestimated toxicities and poor efficacy have been observed in humans. There are a variety of reasons for failure of NATs, one of which is that many preclinical studies lack disease modelling in a human-relevant manner and, therefore, do not capture disease-specific effects on therapy tolerability and efficacy. This Perspective provides a short overview of why better human disease modelling is required to understand the potential therapeutic liabilities of NATs across modalities.

abstract: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a common, often disabling disorder of gut-brain interaction whose molecular basis remains incompletely defined, leaving diagnosis largely symptom-based and treatment largely non-mechanistic. We argue that the serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine; hereafter 5-HT, the primary term used throughout, with "serotonin" retained in less technical contexts) signalling axis-positioned at the interface of the gut microbiota, enterochromaffin (EC) cells, enteric neurons, and the mucosal immune system-is a central, unifying integrator of IBS pathophysiology, and that reframing IBS around this axis offers a route toward mechanism-based subtyping and therapy. We first synthesise how microbiota-driven tryptophan metabolism, short-chain fatty acid and secondary bile acid signalling, and epigenetic regulation of tryptophan hydroxylase 1 (TPH1) shape EC-cell serotonin output, before examining the neuroimmune consequences of dysregulated serotonin secretion-mast cell activation, macrophage polarisation, neurogenic inflammation-and the microbiota-serotonin-gut-brain connectome linking vagal afferent signalling, blood-brain barrier permeability, and central neurotransmitter networks. We then discuss molecular stratification of IBS subtypes through serotonergic endotyping-incorporating SLC6A4 and TPH1 polymorphisms, single-cell transcriptomics, and spatial metabolomics-and critically evaluate next-generation therapeutic strategies, including engineered probiotic chassis, CRISPR-mediated microbial editing, and AI-guided nanomedicine, distinguishing proof-of-concept findings from clinically validated approaches. We conclude that reconceptualising IBS as a disorder of disrupted microbial serotonergic ecosystems, rather than a purely symptom-defined syndrome, offers a coherent and testable framework for biomarker discovery and precision, mechanism-directed therapy, while highlighting the causal-directionality and clinical-translation gaps that must be closed before this framework can be applied at the bedside.

title: Microbial serotonin signalling axes in irritable bowel syndrome: integrative molecular crosstalk among enterochromaffin cells, gut microbiota, neuroimmune circuits, and precision therapeutic engineering.

abstract: Postmenopausal osteoporosis (PO) is not merely a consequence of increased osteoclast activity. Estrogen deficiency induces oxidative stress and pro-inflammatory M1 macrophage polarization in bone tissue, thereby sustaining osteoclastogenic stimuli and pathological bone resorption. Interferon regulatory factor 5 (IRF5) is a key regulator of M1 polarization, and silencing its gene by small interfering RNA (siIRF5) may attenuate the pathogenesis of PO. However, selective delivery of siIRF5 to M1 macrophages within the osteoporotic bone microenvironment is challenging. Herein, we develop a nanomedicine, termed siP@WM, for programmed sequential targeting of bone tissue and macrophages. The siP@WM integrates a platinum nanozyme core with mesoporous silica shell loading siIRF5. The shell with enlarged pores (10-15 nm) provides effective siRNA encapsulation and programmable surface grafting of two kinds of poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) derivatives. The longer poly(aspartic acid)-terminated PEG chain promotes bone enrichment. ROS-triggered thioketal cleavage shortens this chain, reduces bone-matrix adhesion, and exposes the shorter folic acid-functionalized PEG chain to enhance M1 macrophage uptake. In vitro, siP@WM scavenges ROS, facilitates endosomal escape, achieves approximately 60% IRF5 knockdown, and promotes M2 polarization. In ovariectomized mice, systemic administration of siP@WM ameliorates bone loss, restores trabecular microarchitecture and mechanical strength, and shows no overt short-term toxicity in major organs. Transcriptomic and histological analyses support attenuated AP-1-associated inflammatory signaling, suppressed osteoclast differentiation, and modulated extracellular matrix remodeling. Together, programmed siIRF5 delivery to macrophages in bone tissue combined with ROS scavenging restores bone homeostasis and provides an adaptive biomaterial strategy for PO treatment.

title: Osteoporosis treatment via programmed delivery of IRF5 siRNA to macrophages in bone tissue combined with ROS scavenging.

abstract: Spherical nucleic acids (SNAs) are a unique class of nucleic acid nanotherapeutics characterized by densely packed, radially arranged oligonucleotides surrounding a nanoparticle or molecular core, or core-free nanoscale structures. Compared with conventional linear nucleic acids, SNAs exhibit excellent cellular uptake, resistance to nuclease degradation, and efficient target recognition without the help of transfection agents. This review summarizes SNAs' structural diversity, design principles, and the multiscale delivery barriers they encounter. We mainly focus on liposomal SNAs (LSNAs) as programmable platforms for cancer immunotherapy. We emphasize how lipid chemistry, membrane architecture, and anchor stability control lymphoid distribution, immune-cell uptake, antigen presentation, and strong antitumor immunity, rather than seeing lipids as inert carriers. Furthermore, we also discuss current developments in gene silencing, CRISPR-based genome editing, and stimulus-responsive multimodal therapies, highlighting the significant therapeutic advancements of SNAs like clinical trial NU-0129 and LSNAs like cavrotolimod. Finally, we describe present translational obstacles and potential prospects by using SNAs as next-generation precision immunotherapeutics.

title: Potential Therapeutic Applications of Spherical Nucleic Acids (SNAs) in Cancer: Key Observations and Insights.

abstract: Retinal degenerative diseases, including age-related macular degeneration (AMD), retinitis pigmentosa (RP), and Stargardt disease, represent leading causes of irreversible vision loss worldwide, collectively affecting hundreds of millions of people. Cell-based therapies, particularly those leveraging induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) transplantation, and CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, have emerged as promising treatment modalities that may preserve, replace, or partially restore retinal function. However, these approaches face significant challenges in patient stratification, manufacturing consistency, surgical precision, and long-term outcome monitoring. Artificial intelligence (AI), encompassing machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and computer vision, is increasingly being integrated across the cell therapy pipeline to address these limitations. This review comprehensively explores the role of AI in enhancing cell-based retinal therapies, spanning disease diagnosis and patient selection, stem cell quality control and differentiation optimization, CRISPR off-target detection, retinal organoid characterization, scalable manufacturing, and post-transplantation monitoring through multimodal retinal imaging. Throughout, we distinguish direct retinal cell-therapy evidence from retinal-adjacent, cross-domain, and conceptual evidence. We also propose an AI-powered end-to-end pipeline that connects patient profiling through gene editing, cell production, and transplantation to longitudinal outcomes tracking (a forward-looking framework that needs to be clinically validated in future). While AI offers powerful tools to enhance efficacy, reproducibility, and personalization, it does not replace the clinical and biological foundations of cell therapy. Critical challenges remain, including data scarcity, algorithmic interpretability, regulatory compliance, and clinical validation. This review concludes that the strategic integration of AI has plausible potential to become supportive infrastructure for scalable and reproducible cell-based treatments for retinal diseases, although its necessity has not been demonstrated and prospective clinical validation is still required, and biological insight and rigorous empirical verification remain fundamental.

abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have risen to the forefront of modern therapeutics by enabling the clinical success of COVID-19 mRNA vaccines. In order for them to function as drug delivery vesicles, LNPs must have scalable, tunable, and targeted nanoscale platforms whose strengths in versatility, performance, and clinical relevance are driven by key design parameters and formulation strategies. This Tutorial Review traces the historical evolution of LNPs and examines the fundamental design principles governing their structure, physicochemical properties, and biological behavior. It further highlights modern analytical characterization techniques that have advanced mechanistic understanding of LNP composition, morphology, and function as well as targeting strategies to improve LNP delivery to extrahepatic sites. Current translational challenges and emerging advances are also discussed. This Tutorial Review provides a framework for understanding the foundations, current landscape, and future directions of LNP research.

abstract: MYC is among the most frequently amplified oncogenes in human cancer, yet its intrinsically disordered nature has rendered it refractory to direct pharmacological targeting. Here, we demonstrate that the long noncoding RNA NEAT1_1 functions as a molecular gatekeeper that controls MYC protein stability by regulating its access to the E3 ubiquitin ligase UBR5. We show that NEAT1_1 forms a ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex with both MYC and UBR5, and that NEAT1_1 suppression disrupts this interaction, leading to decreased MYC polyubiquitination and enhanced protein stability. To systematically map the regulatory architecture of NEAT1_1 without altering its abundance, we screened 88 antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) mixmers tiling across the transcript. Strikingly, this phenotypic screen identified region-specific mixmers that elicit bidirectional control over MYC, either driving robust MYC destabilization or promoting its stabilization in a strictly expression-independent manner. Mechanistically, MYC-destabilizing mixmers selectively enhance the interaction between MYC and UBR5 to accelerate proteasomal degradation. A focused CRISPR screen targeting the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway independently validated UBR5 as the essential E3 ligase mediating this mixmer-induced turnover. In vivo, our lead mixmer ASO_#24 significantly suppressed tumor growth in MYC-high xenografts, whereas MYC-low tumors remained unaffected. Our findings reveal that the functional output of a scaffold lncRNA is encoded in its sub-domain architecture rather than bulk transcript levels, establishing domain-specific RNA targeting as a tractable strategy to rewire protein turnover pathways for otherwise undruggable oncogenes.

title: NEAT1 remodeling rewires the MYC degradation pathway.

abstract:
AIMS: Selenoprotein T (SELENOT) is an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-resident thioredoxin-like oxidoreductase implicated in redox and calcium (Ca2+) homeostasis and protein quality control. Although SELENOT is highly expressed in the brain, its role in hypothalamic pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons, which regulate energy balance, remains poorly understood. We investigated whether SELENOT is required for maintaining ER homeostasis and neuronal integrity in POMC neurons.
RESULTS: Using CRISPR-edited and siRNA-silenced POMC neuronal models together with a POMC-specific SELENOT knockout mouse, we demonstrated that SELENOT loss induces a senescent-like phenotype including cellular hypertrophy, loss of neurite outgrowth, senescence-associated β-galactosidase activity, increased P16 and P21 expression, and acquisition of senescence-associated secretory phenotype. Senescence markers were elevated not only in SELENOT-deficient POMC neurons but also throughout the surrounding arcuate nucleus in vivo, suggesting propagation of a pro-inflammatory microenvironment. Mechanistically, prolonged SELENOT deficiency produced selective activation of the ATF6α arm of the unfolded protein response, depletion of ER Ca2+ stores, and profound alterations in N-glycan maturation. Notably, leptin-induced POMC processing and secretion were spared. Glycomics revealed a shift toward immature glycans, whereas thiol-trapping proteomics identified candidate SELENOT interactors linked to ER Ca2+ regulation.
INNOVATION AND CONCLUSIONS: This study provides the first evidence that SELENOT deficiency is sufficient to trigger cellular senescence in POMC neurons, acting as a central regulator integrating ER proteostasis, Ca2+ homeostasis, redox adaptation, and glycosylation. These results reveal a previously unrecognized mechanism potentially linking neuronal senescence to hypothalamic dysfunction and suggest that SELENOT-dependent pathways may represent therapeutic targets for obesity, metabolic disease, and age-related neuroendocrine disorders. Antioxid. Redox Signal. 00, 000-000.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed the management of mismatch repair-deficient/microsatellite instability-high (dMMR/MSI-H) colorectal cancer (CRC), yet the ~95% of patients with mismatch repair-proficient/microsatellite-stable (pMMR/MSS) disease derive little benefit owing to an immunologically "cold" tumor microenvironment (TME), poor T-cell infiltration, myeloid dominance, TGF-β-enriched stroma, and the systemically immunosuppressive milieu imposed by hepatic metastases. Clinically tested combinations-multikinase inhibitor plus anti-PD-1, Fc-enhanced dual checkpoint blockade, chemotherapy- or antiangiogenic-ICI regimens-have so far produced modest, largely non-durable response rates that are further attenuated in liver-metastatic disease, motivating approaches that pharmacologically remodel the TME rather than only release checkpoint restraint.
OBJECTIVE: To provide an evidence-stratified synthesis of nanotechnology-enabled immunotherapy in CRC that explicitly separates (a) clinically established evidence, (b) strategies under early-phase clinical investigation, and (c) concepts that remain preclinical or are extrapolated from other tumor types, and to derive from this appraisal a biomarker-enriched translational research agenda.
METHODS: Narrative, integrative (non-systematic) review. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ASCO/ESMO/AACR proceedings were searched from January 2010 through April 2026. Each strategy was appraised according to the highest available level of evidence, the tumor type and model system in which the evidence was generated, and its demonstrated CRC specificity.
RESULTS: In current clinical practice, nanomedicine in CRC is essentially limited to nanoparticle-formulated cytotoxics exploited for pharmacokinetic advantage (e.g. liposomal irinotecan), whereas nano-enabled immunotherapy is confined to a small number of early-phase trials-most notably lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-formulated individualized neoantigen mRNA vaccines in ctDNA-positive resected CRC and hafnium-oxide nanoparticle radioenhancers-none of which has yet demonstrated a progression-free or overall survival benefit in MSS CRC. Against this background we critically appraise six classes of strategy: (i) LNP-based mRNA neoantigen vaccines; (ii) polymeric and inorganic nanocarriers for STING and TLR agonists; (iii) tumor-associated macrophage-repolarizing nanoparticles; (iv) nano-radiosensitizers and photothermal/photodynamic platforms priming immunogenic cell death; (v) nano-formulated checkpoint inhibitor delivery; and (vi) locoregional nano-strategies directed at hepatic metastasis-specific immunosuppression. For categories (ii)-(vi) the supporting evidence is predominantly murine (largely subcutaneous CT26/MC38 models) or extrapolated from immunologically "hot" tumors such as melanoma and non-small-cell lung cancer, in which both the underlying biology and the checkpoint backbone differ materially from MSS CRC. Recurrent translational barriers include low, highly heterogeneous nanoparticle accumulation in human tumors, dense TGF-β-rich stroma and elevated interstitial pressure, mononuclear phagocyte system clearance, liver-metastasis-specific tolerance that subcutaneous models do not reproduce, unresolved manufacturing/CMC and regulatory pathways, and the absence of validated pharmacodynamic biomarkers of intratumoral immune conversion.
CONCLUSION: Nanotechnology offers a mechanistically coherent and experimentally testable-but at present clinically unproven-set of strategies for converting "cold" MSS CRC into immune-responsive disease. We therefore position nano-enabled immunotherapy as a research priority rather than an imminent standard of care, and argue that its clinical value can only be established through biomarker-enriched, paired-biopsy early-phase trials with pharmacodynamic endpoints of immune conversion and prospective stratification by metastatic site (particularly hepatic involvement) and consensus molecular subtype.
LIMITATIONS: This is a narrative rather than systematic review; it is therefore subject to selection and publication bias, and much of the evidence synthesized is preclinical and of limited direct translational certainty.

abstract: Probe-based PCR assays are commonly used to evaluate gene expression in antisense oligonucleotide (ASO)-treated samples, but assay design and postextraction processing may introduce substantial measurement bias. We investigated workflow-dependent differences in measured knockdown across PCR-based and RNA-sequencing assays using an allele-specific gapmer ASO, targeting a linked single nucleotide polymorphism of a dominant-negative SPTAN1 variant. Exogenous ribonuclease H (RNase H) activity during reverse transcription or ribosomal RNA (rRNA)-depletion inflated apparent knockdown and reduced RNA-sequencing coverage at the ASO-binding site. In droplet digital PCR (ddPCR), allele-specific detection probes overlapping the ASO-binding site produced substantially greater apparent knockdown than nonoverlapping probes, particularly following workflows with active RNase H. Spike-in experiments showed that this bias was not reproduced by adding ASO to purified RNA before complementary DNA (cDNA) synthesis or to cDNA before ddPCR, but emerged when ASO was present during rRNA depletion. Together, these findings show that exogenous RNase H activity during RNA processing and ASO-probe overlap can distort measurements of gapmer-mediated transcript reduction. Poly(A)-based RNA sequencing, reverse transcriptase with reduced RNase H activity, and nonoverlapping PCR detection probes can minimize measurement bias when evaluating gapmer ASO-mediated knockdown.

title: Considerations of Gene Expression Analysis Methods for Gapmer Antisense Oligonucleotide-Treated Samples.

abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a major cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Emerging evidence has established N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA methylation as a key epitranscriptomic mechanism underlying hepatocarcinogenesis. Methyltransferase-like 3 (METTL3), the catalytic core of the m6A methyltransferase complex (MTC), forms a heterodimer with METTL14 and cooperates with auxiliary components of the MTC to deposit m6A modifications that modulate mRNA stability, splicing, nuclear export, and translation. In this review, we comprehensively summarize the current understanding of METTL3 biology in HCC, focusing on its structure, assembly within the MTC, regulation of coding and non-coding RNAs, and its roles in driving key oncogenic signaling cascades, such as JAK/STAT3, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, Wnt/β-catenin, Hippo/YAP, Notch, Hedgehog, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. In addition, we discussed how METTL3 remodels the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) by regulating immune responses and metabolic pathways promoting immune evasion and therapy resistance. Therapeutic strategies targeting METTL3-including small-molecule inhibitors, CRISPR-Cas9 approaches, combination immunotherapy, and tumor-selective delivery systems-are discussed together with the challenges that continue to limit clinical translation. Collectively, these findings position METTL3 as a central epitranscriptomic regulator of HCC progression; however, further mechanistic and clinical validation remains necessary to establish its utility as a therapeutic target and prognostic biomarker.

title: The Role of METTL3-Mediated m6A Methylation in Hepatocellular Carcinoma Progression and Treatment.

abstract:
Background:

Warts, hypogammaglobulinemia, infections and myelokathexis syndrome (WHIMs) is a rare disorder that affects the immune system. People with WHIMs can have severe infections all over their body. WHIMs is caused by a mutation in the CXCR4 gene. Treatment with drugs can help control the infections but does not cure the disorder. Researchers want to try a treatment where they collect stem cells from a person with WHIMS, use base-editing to replace the bad gene with a healthy version, and return the new cells to the person. This could cure WHIMs.

Objective:

To test a treatment using base-edited stem cells in people with WHIMs.

Eligibility:

People aged 3 years and older with WHIMs.

Design:

The study has 4 stages.

Stage 1: Screening. Participants will be screened at 1 or more visits. They will have a physical exam with blood tests. A sample of tissue and fluid (biopsy) will be taken from the bone marrow in the hip.

Stage 2: Apheresis. Blood will be taken from the body through a needle; the blood will pass through a machine that separates out the stem cells. The remaining blood will be returned to the body through a different needle. The collected stem cells will undergo gene editing.

Stage 3: Treatment. Participants will stay in the hospital for about 4 weeks. They will receive 3 drugs to prepare their body for the procedure. Then the edited stem cells will be returned to their bloodstream. They will stay in the hospital until they recover.

Stage 4: Follow-up. Participants will have 8 follow-up visits over 5 years. Long-term visits will continue for 15 years.

description:
Study Description:

This is a phase 1/2, non-randomized study of a single infusion of autologous hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells (HSPC) base-edited to repair CXCR4 mutations in 10 participants with (Warts, Hypogammaglobulinemia, Infections, and Myelokathexis) WHIM syndrome.

Primary Objective: Evaluate safety of treatment with BE-HSPC CXCR4 in participants with WHIM syndrome.

Secondary Objectives:

Evaluate:

* Efficacy.
* Genetic correction.
* Immune reconstitution.
* Clinical efficacy.

Exploratory Objective:

Evaluate off-target (OT) editing activity.

Primary Endpoint:

Safety assessed by:

* Incidence of adverse events (AEs) for each participant.
* Evaluate overall incidence of AEs for the study.
* Incidence of serious adverse events (SAEs).

Secondary Endpoints (24 months post-study agent infusion):

* Efficacy: \>= 5% gene edited circulating myeloid cells by 12 months after BE HSPC infusion.
* Gene correction:

  --Frequency of corrected alleles in peripheral blood cells (such as myeloid, T, B, and natural killer \[NK\] cells).

  --\>200/microL edited neutrophils by 12 months post receipt of the BE HSPC infusion.
* Immune reconstitution:

  * T, B, and NK cell number improvement from baseline.
  * B-cell function: immunoglobulin (Ig) production.
* Clinical efficacy: Improvement from baseline problems such as recurrent infection, wart burden, gastrointestinal complaints, or immune dysregulation.

Exploratory Endpoint:

Evaluate for frequency of OTs by high-throughput sequencing (HTS) of the target mutation at the genomic locus 2 years post-infusion.

abstract: Some, but not all, gapmer antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) delivered into cerebrospinal fluid exhibit fatal subacute toxicity in late-stage prion-infected mice but not in uninfected mice. Here, we performed a battery of in vivo studies demonstrating that the toxicity is compound- and disease- stage-dependent, and not predicted by behavioral or molecular measurements in uninfected animals. A panel of toxic ASOs all elicited a consistent transcriptomic response signature in prion-infected mice, which emerged over the course of 7 days post dose. This signature, driven chiefly by decreased expression of a specific set of astrocyte-expressed genes, was absent in uninfected mice receiving the same ASOs, was absent, less intense, and/or more transient in infected mice receiving tolerated ASOs, and was distinct from the transcriptomic effect of prion disease itself. Our data argue that the toxicity is an interaction between ASO and prion disease at high doses for specific compounds, and does not represent an exacerbation of ASO toxicity nor of prion disease.

title: Antisense Oligonucleotides that Are Toxic to Prion-Infected Mice Share an Emergent Mechanism.

abstract: In this study, we developed a library of mRNA lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) containing clinically used ionizable lipids. We surface-modified these nanoparticles with heparosan polysaccharides and systematically compared their performance with conventional poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG)-modified formulations. Our heparosan (HEP)-coated LNPs increased mRNA expression in dendritic and macrophage cell lines by up to ∼10-fold. Mechanistic studies using live-cell imaging and intracellular nanoparticle trafficking analysis revealed that HEP-modified LNPs exhibited reduced colocalization with late endosomal (Rab7+) and lysosomal (LAMP1+) compartments. These findings are consistent with enhanced endosomal escape of HEP-modified formulations. Repeated subcutaneous administrations of HEP-modified firefly luciferase mRNA-LNPs demonstrated sustained expression and distinct response dynamics in mice. We further observed significantly enhanced humoral anti-spike protein immune responses in mice after subcutaneous administration of HEP-modified LNPs containing SARS-CoV-2 spike S-2P mRNA. Histopathological evaluation and spleen immune cell profiling showed no observable toxicity or adverse effects. Overall, these results demonstrate the effects of HEP surface modification on mRNA LNP expression, intracellular trafficking, and in vivo activity, and support HEP-based surface engineering as a PEG-free approach for nucleic acid delivery and potential future applications in nanomedicine.

title: Lipid Nanoparticle Surface Engineering with Heparosan Polysaccharides Enhances mRNA Efficacy via Reduced Endosomal Retention.

abstract: This phase III trial tests how well the addition of dinutuximab to Induction chemotherapy along with standard of care surgical resection of the primary tumor, radiation, stem cell transplantation, and immunotherapy works for treating children with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma. Dinutuximab is a monoclonal antibody that binds to a molecule called GD2, which is found on the surface of neuroblastoma cells, but is not present on many healthy or normal cells in the body. When dinutuximab binds to the neuroblastoma cells, it helps signal the immune system to kill the tumor cells. This helps the cells of the immune system kill the cancer cells, this is a type of immunotherapy. When chemotherapy and immunotherapy are given together, during the same treatment cycle, it is called chemoimmunotherapy. This clinical trial randomly assigns patients to receive either standard chemotherapy and surgery or chemoimmunotherapy (chemotherapy plus dinutuximab) and surgery during Induction therapy. Chemotherapy drugs administered during Induction include, cyclophosphamide, topotecan, cisplatin, etoposide, vincristine, and doxorubicin. These drugs work in different ways to stop the growth of cancer cells, either by killing the cells, by stopping them from dividing or by stopping them from spreading. Upon completion of 5 cycles of Induction therapy, a disease evaluation is completed to determine how well the treatment worked. If the tumor responds to therapy, patients receive a tandem transplantation with stem cell rescue. If the tumor has little improvement or worsens, patients receive chemoimmunotherapy on Extended Induction. During Extended Induction, dinutuximab is given with irinotecan, temozolomide. Patients with a good response to therapy move on to Consolidation therapy, when very high doses of chemotherapy are given at two separate points to kill any remaining cancer cells. Following, transplant, radiation therapy is given to the site where the cancer originated (primary site) and to any other areas that are still active at the end of Induction. The final stage of therapy is Post-Consolidation. During Post-Consolidation, dinutuximab is given with isotretinoin, with the goal of maintaining the response achieved with the previous therapy. Adding dinutuximab to Induction chemotherapy along with standard of care surgical resection of the primary tumor, radiation, stem cell transplantation, and immunotherapy may be better at treating children with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma.
description:
PRIMARY OBJECTIVE:

I. To determine if the event-free survival (EFS) of patients with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma assigned to early chemoimmunotherapy during Induction differs from that of patients who are not assigned to treatment that includes early chemoimmunotherapy.

SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To determine if early chemoimmunotherapy during Induction therapy improves end of Induction (EOI) response rates and overall survival (OS) for patients with newly diagnosed high-risk neuroblastoma.

II. To determine response rates, EFS, and OS following an Extended Induction regimen with chemoimmunotherapy in patients with progressive disease or a poor response to Induction therapy.

III. To compare the toxicities experienced by patients treated with chemoimmunotherapy during Induction versus those experienced by patients treated with standard Induction and to describe toxicities experienced during Extended Induction.

IV. To determine GD2 expression on tumor tissue and tumor cells in bone marrow and assess for associations with response and outcome.

EXPLORATORY OBJECTIVES:

I. To describe the association between tumor and host factors and outcomes in patients receiving protocol therapy.

II. To evaluate circulating biomarkers and markers of minimal residual disease at baseline and during therapy, and assess for associations with response and outcome.

III. To compare patterns of failure between patients treated with and without dinutuximab during induction.

IV. To determine the effect of telomere maintenance mechanisms on end of Induction response rates, EFS, and OS.

V. To explore the impact of high-risk neuroblastoma (HRNBL) and its therapy, including the addition of dinutuximab to Induction chemotherapy, on functional and quality of life outcomes in patients with HRNBL, as measured by caregiver (parent/legal guardian) and patient questionnaires.

VI. To describe the adequacy of diagnostic biopsy specimens, including those obtained by percutaneous core needle biopsy.

VII. To explore the associations between family-reported adverse social determinants of health and both clinical outcomes and biology.

VIII. To develop and validate deep learning predictors of Induction response based on diagnostic MIBG scans. (Imaging Objective) IX. To compare institutional versus central determination of overall response, individual response components (primary tumor, soft tissue and bone metastatic disease, and bone marrow metastatic disease), and poor end of induction response (PEIR) and good end of induction response (GEIR) determination. (Imaging Objective) X. To describe late toxicities (including impaired organ function, neuropsychiatric toxicity, and incidence of secondary malignancy) in patients treated with dinutuximab during Induction or Extended Induction to late toxicities in patients who have not received dinutuximab during these phases of therapy.

XI. To evaluate whether reduced dose radiotherapy to the primary site clinical target volume (CTV) in patients with complete response of the primary site at EOI results in comparable local control relative to historical cohorts.

XII. To compare post-transplant complications between treatment arms, and assess for associations with outcome.

XIII. To assess for associations between EOI response (including good end of Induction response \[GEIR\] and poor end of Induction response \[PEIR\]) and individual response components (primary tumor, soft tissue and bone metastatic disease, and bone marrow metastatic disease) with outcome (EFS and OS).

XIV. To describe and compare the changes in image-defined risk factors (IDRFs) between patients treated with and without dinutuximab during Induction and associate with surgical outcomes and local failure rates following primary tumor resection.

XV. To bank serial samples of blood, bone marrow, and tumor tissue for future research.

OUTLINE: Patients receive Induction cycle 1 and are then randomized to 1 of 2 treatment arms.

INDUCTION CYCLE 1: Patients receive cyclophosphamide intravenously (IV) over 30 minutes and topotecan IV over 30 minutes on days 1-5 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity.

ARM A:

INDUCTION CYCLES 2-5: Patients receive cyclophosphamide IV over 30 minutes and topotecan IV over 30 minutes on days 1-5 of cycle 2 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients then undergo stem cell harvest via apheresis. Patients then receive cisplatin IV over 4 hours and etoposide IV over 2 hours on days 1-3 of cycles 3 and 5, and vincristine IV on day 1, doxorubicin IV over 15 minutes, and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days 1-2 of cycle 4 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients undergo primary tumor resection after Induction cycle 4 or 5. Following Induction cycle 5, patients undergo testing to determine response to Induction therapy. Patients with a good tumor response proceed to Consolidation, while patients with a poor tumor response proceed to Extended Induction.

EXTENDED INDUCTION: Patients with a poor tumor response or progression during Induction receive temozolomide orally (PO), via nasogastric tube (NG), or via gastric tube (G-tube) on days 1-5, irinotecan IV over 90 minutes on days 1-5, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours. Treatment repeats every 21 days for up to a maximum of 6 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. If at any time during Extended Induction testing shows a good tumor response, patients proceed to Consolidation. If after 6 cycles of Extended Induction or if at any time progression is noted, patients are removed from the study.

CONSOLIDATION: Patients undergo two autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantations (HSCTs) during Consolidation. Patients receive thiotepa IV over 2 hours on days -7 to -5 and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days -5 to -2 during HSCT 1. Patients then receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between 6 and 10 weeks after stem cell infusion, patients receive melphalan IV over 30 minutes on days -7 to -5, etoposide IV over 24 hours on days -7 to -4, and carboplatin over 24 hours on days -7 to -4 during HSCT 2. Patients receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between day +42 and day +80 after HSCT 2. Patients receive radiation daily for 12 treatments in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity.

POST CONSOLIDATION: Patients receive dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 4-7 and isotretinoin PO twice daily (BID) on days 11-24 of cycles 1-5. Treatment repeats every 28 days for up to 5 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Patients then receive isotretinoin PO BID on days 15-28 for 1 additional cycle, cycle 6.

Patients undergo blood and urine sample collection, echocardiogram (ECHO) or multigated acquisition scan (MUGA), bone marrow aspiration and/or biopsy, computed tomography (CT) scan, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), iodine-123 meta-iodobenzylguanidine (I-MIBG) scan and possible fluorodeoxyglucose position emission tomography (FDG-PET) scan throughout the study.

ARM B:

INDUCTION CYCLES 2-5: Patients receive cyclophosphamide IV over 30 minutes, topotecan IV over 30 minutes on days 1-5, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 2-5 of cycle 2 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients then undergo stem cell harvest via apheresis. Patients receive cisplatin IV over 4 hours and etoposide IV over 2 hours on days 1-3 and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 2-5 of cycles 3 and 5, and vincristine IV on day 1, doxorubicin IV over 15 minutes, and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days 1-2, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 2-5 of cycle 4 in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Patients undergo primary tumor resection after Induction cycle 4 or 5. Following Induction cycle 5, patients undergo testing to determine response to Induction therapy. Patients with a good tumor response proceed to Consolidation, while patients with a poor tumor response proceed to Extended Induction.

EXTENDED INDUCTION: Patients with a poor tumor response or progression during Induction receive temozolomide PO, via NG tube, or via G-tube on days 1-5, irinotecan IV over 90 minutes on days 1-5, and dinutuximab IV over 10 hours. Treatment repeats every 21 days for up to a maximum of 6 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. If at any time during Extended Induction testing shows a good tumor response, patients proceed to Consolidation. If after 6 cycles of Extended Induction or if at any time progression is noted, patients are removed from the study.

CONSOLIDATION: Patients undergo two autologous HSCTs during Consolidation. Patients receive thiotepa IV over 2 hours on days -7 to -5 and cyclophosphamide IV over 1 hour on days -5 to -2 during HSCT 1. Patients then receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between 6 and 10 weeks after stem cell infusion patients receive melphalan IV over 30 minutes on days -7 to -5, etoposide IV over 24 hours on days -7 to -4, and carboplatin over 24 hours on days -7 to -4 during HSCT 2. Patients receive stem cell infusion IV on day 0. Between day +42 and day +80 after HSCT 2, patients receive radiation daily for 12 treatments in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity.

POST CONSOLIDATION: Patients receive dinutuximab IV over 10 hours on days 4-7 and isotretinoin PO BID on days 11-24 of cycles 1-5. Treatment repeats every 28 days for up to 5 cycles in the absence of disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. Patients then receive isotretinoin PO BID on days 15-28 for 1 additional cycle, cycle 6.

Patients undergo blood and urine sample collection, ECHO or MUGA, bone marrow aspiration and/or biopsy, CT scan, MRI, I-MIBG scan and possible FDG-PET scan throughout the study.

After completion of study treatment, patients are followed up at 3, 6, 9,12, 15, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 54, and 60 months and then periodically for up to 10 years from enrollment.

outcomes.description: EFS time is calculated from time of randomization to Arms A or B to first episode of disease relapse or progression, second malignancy, or death, or until last contact if no event has occurred.
outcomes.measure: Event free survival (EFS)

outcomes.description: The response rate will be calculated among all evaluable patients at end of Induction. Responders are defined as patients who achieve a \>= partial response per the revised 2017 International Neuroblastoma Response Criteria (INRC)
outcomes.measure: End of Induction (EOI) response rate
outcomes.time_frame: From randomization to end of extended Induction, up to 12 months

outcomes.description: OS time is calculated from time of randomization to Arms A or B until death, or until last contact if patient is alive.
outcomes.measure: Overall survival (OS)

outcomes.description: The proportion of patients with at least one grade 3 or higher non-hematologic toxicity or grade 4 or higher hematologic toxicity during protocol therapy, graded according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0, will be reported.
outcomes.measure: Incidence of adverse events

outcomes.description: Dinutuximab binding to pre-therapy patient tumor samples will be measured and categorized as high or low.
outcomes.measure: GD2 expression

outcomes.description: A series of univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards (for EFS and OS) and logistic regression (for responders vs. non-responders) models will be fit for patients in Arms A and B to evaluate the relationship between tumor and host factors (including tumor ALK and other somatic mutations, copy-number aberrations, gene fusions, gene expression, and pathogenic germline variants) and chemo-immunotherapy during Induction with outcome.
outcomes.measure: Association between tumor and host factors and outcomes

outcomes.description: Will be assessed by comparing the proportion of patients with detectable vs. non-detectable tumor markers (including circulating tumor deoxyribonucleic acid, circulating free DNA, circulating tumor cells, and immune function profiling) between Arms A and B during and after induction and post-consolidation therapy using chi-squared tests at each individual time point, and Cochran's Q across time points to determine if there is a consistent difference in proportions between arms across time. In addition, the tumor markers will be analyzed as continuous variables using longitudinal data analysis methodology such as mixed effects models or generalized estimating equations as appropriate.
outcomes.measure: Circulating biomarkers and markers of minimal residual disease

outcomes.description: The impact of early or late chemoimmunotherapy during Induction on the probability of the involvement of a specific disease site at first relapse will be evaluated using Fisher's exact test.
outcomes.measure: Patterns of failure

outcomes.description: A series of univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards (for EFS and OS) and logistic regression (for responders vs. non-responders) models will be fit for patients in arms A and B to evaluate the relationship between telomere maintenance mechanism and chemoimmunotherapy during Induction with outcome. Patients will be classified into 3 groups by telomere maintenance mechanism (TMM) based on messenger ribonucleic acid expression of TERT and analysis of telomeric DNA C-circles: telomerase (TERT) positive, alternative of lengthening of telomeres (ALT) positive, or no identified TMM.
outcomes.measure: Effect of telomere maintenance mechanisms

outcomes.description: Will descriptively summarize and compare the total Memorial Symptom Assessment Scale scores, total sub-domain scores, and individual symptom scores between patients randomized to receive dinutuximab during Induction (Arm B) to those of patients randomized to standard Induction (Arm A).
outcomes.measure: Functional and quality of life outcomes
outcomes.time_frame: At serial time points during Induction, Extended Induction, Post-Consolidation, and at the end of therapy

outcomes.description: Will be evaluated by descriptively comparing the successful delineation of histologic classification, MYCN amplification status, and ALK status via the traditional method of obtaining tissue for diagnosis, open surgical biopsy, versus the less invasive percutaneous core needle biopsy.
outcomes.measure: Adequacy of diagnostic biopsy specimens

outcomes.description: Kaplan-Meier curves of EFS and OS will be generated and used to calculate 3-year EFS and OS estimates. Associations between social determinants of health (SDOH) and survival outcomes and time to receipt of dinutuximab will be evaluated with univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazard models. Log-binomial regression will be used to estimate risk ratios and 95% CI for the occurrence of dinutuximab consent to randomization and therapy receipt by SDOH exposure. Effect modification of outcomes as a function of poverty, stratified by race/ethnicity, will be explored.
outcomes.measure: Associations between family-reported adverse social determinants of health and both clinical outcomes and biology

outcomes.description: Scans will be given as input to a convolutional neural network trained to predict EOI response.
outcomes.measure: Develop and validate deep learning predictors of Induction response (imaging objective)
outcomes.time_frame: At diagnosis, EOI, during Extended Induction, and end of Extended Induction

outcomes.description: Will be assessed by calculating the percentage of patients receiving the same EOI institutional and centrally reviewed determination of overall response, individual response components (primary tumor, soft tissue and bone metastatic disease, and bone marrow metastatic disease), and PEIR and GEIR. In addition, Cohen's kappa will be calculated to evaluate the concordance in each of these response measures.
outcomes.measure: Compare institutional versus central determination of overall response, individual response components, and PEIR and GEIR determination (imaging objective)

outcomes.description: Will be addressed by calculating the proportion of treated patients with each late effect, including but not limited to impaired organ function, neuropsychiatric toxicity, and secondary malignancy. A 95% confidence interval will be placed on each proportion.
outcomes.measure: Incidence of late toxicities

outcomes.description: The cumulative incidence of local progression (CILP) in patients with complete response of the primary site at EOI and GEIR on this study will be compared to the CILP rate of 11.2±1.8% observed on ANBL0532 using Gray's test.
outcomes.measure: Reduced dose radiotherapy to the primary site clinical target volume (CTV) in patients with complete response of the primary site at EOI results in comparable local control relative to historical cohorts

outcomes.description: Will be evaluated by calculating the incidence of endothelial injury complications and non-relapse mortality within 100 days of transplant, transplant-associated thrombotic microangiopathy (TA-TMA), severe TA-TMA, and sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (SOS) on Arms A and B and comparing between arms with a chi-squared test. The impact of TA-TMA occurrence on the timing or exclusion of subsequent therapy and interventions utilized to treat the TA-TMA, and associations with outcomes (EFS and OS) will be assessed.
outcomes.measure: Post-transplant complications

outcomes.description: Log-rank tests will be used to explore the association between EOI response (using both the revised INRC and GEIR/PEIR classification) and individual response components (primary tumor, soft tissue and bone metastatic disease, and bone marrow metastatic disease) with outcome (EFS and OS).
outcomes.measure: Associations between end of induction (EOI) response and individual response components

outcomes.description: The proportion of patients in the analytic cohort for whom each particular IDRF and also the presence of any IDRF is absent prior to surgical resection will be computed. McNemar's test for paired observations will be applied to determine whether there is a difference in the proportion of each IDRF and any IDRF present before and after initial therapy, and conditional logistic regression will be used to compare between treatment arms A and B. The IDRF status after initial therapy and whether there has been a change from diagnosis will be associated with surgical outcome (complete vs. incomplete resection, presence or absence of surgical complications) using chi-squared tests, and compared between treatment arms A and B with the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test. The association of IDRF status with presence or absence of local failure after primary tumor resection will also be evaluated using a chi-squared test, and compared between treatment arms A and B with the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel.
outcomes.measure: Changes in image-defined risk factors (IDRF)

description: In observational studies, small daily doses of lithium have been associated with a 77% reduced risk of developing Parkinson's disease (PD). In addition, lithium therapy has been effective in preventing neuronal death and behavioral symptoms in several PD animal models. Recently, our group has shown 24-weeks of low-dose lithium therapy in PD to improve both MRI and blood-based biomarkers implying that lithium may be slowing the progression of the disease. However, these findings stem from only three of four patients receiving MRIs. A larger study will be required to determine if these promising results can be replicated. The proposed study will enroll 20 additional PD patients who will be randomly assigned to receive either lithium 20mg/day or identically-appearing placebo capsules for 24 weeks. This will be a double-blind study meaning that neither the patients nor the study team will know to which therapy patients have been assigned. Positive results from this study will support further research on lithium that could eventually support lithium as a disease-modifying therapy for PD that could improve patients' long-term prognoses.

description: In observational studies, small daily doses of lithium from smoking cigarettes have been associated with a 77% reduced risk of developing Parkinson's disease (PD). In addition, lithium therapy has been effective in preventing neuronal death and behavioral symptoms in several PD animal models. Recently, our group has shown 24-weeks of low-dose lithium therapy in PD to be associated with improvements in both MRI and blood-based biomarkers implying that lithium may be slowing the progression of the disease. However, these findings stemmed from only three of four patients receiving MRIs. Our group is now conducting two larger studies enrolling a total of 35 PD patients who are being treated with either 45mg/day or 20mg/day of lithium or placebo therapy for 24 weeks. Because our earlier study showed maximum improvements in PD biomarkers in patients with serum lithium levels of 0.25-0.50mmol/L and there are large interpatient variations in serum lithium levels achieved from the same lithium dosage, this present study will adjust lithium dosing in each patient to achieve this target serum lithium level for an additional 24 weeks. MRI and blood-based biomarker changes from Baseline will be compared in patients with serum lithium levels ≥ 0.25mmol/L and \<0.25mmol/L from one of the 24-week studies and within individual patients. Results from this study may identify a target serum lithium level range associated with maximum improvements in PD biomarkers that can be used in the design of future, larger lithium PD lithium trials, which may eventually support lithium as a disease-modifying therapy for PD that could improve patients' long-term prognoses.

abstract: Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) has demonstrated clinical efficacy in advanced HER2-low to -ultralow breast cancer. We employed a mouse model of triple-negative breast cancer in the difficult-to-treat brain metastasis setting to determine T-DXd efficacy and investigate mechanism(s). T-DXd (10 and 3 mg/kg) was compared to an identical ADC except HER2-nonbinding (control) in a hematogenous model of HER2-ultralow brain-tropic triple-negative breast cancer, MDA-MB-231-BR7 (231-BR). The roles of HER2 and the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) were determined by CRISPR-Cas9 deletion and shRNA knockdown, respectively. 231-BR cells exhibited HER2 0+ staining, with occasional membrane expression. T-DXd at 10 mg/kg reduced 231-BR brain metastases by 49% (P=0.002), while a dose reduction showed a 30% (ns) metastasis reduction, each compared to the control-ADC. HER2-specific and -nonspecific ADC uptake into metastases was accompanied by a 23-47% tumor cell Ki-67 decline, and 5-fold increase in tumor apoptosis. A HER2 CRISPR-Cas9 knockout 231-BR formed multiple brain metastases but was insensitive to T-DXd in vivo. 231-BR tumor cells expressed FcRn, potentially enabling nonspecific ADC uptake. Analysis of human tumors showed TNBC tumors expressed FcRn mRNA. T-DXd failed to inhibit brain metastases in two 231-BR FcRn knockdown clones compared to a 231-BR clone transduced with a scrambled shRNA where T-DXd inhibited brain metastases (67% reduction, P=0.01). Despite ultralow HER2 expression, the HER2 binding capacity of T-DXd is a significant contributor to its efficacy. Breast cancers variably express FcRn, suggesting that nonspecific tumor cell uptake of T-DXd via FcRn is also a potential mechanism of T-DXd action.

abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy has revolutionized the treatment of B cell malignancies, and extending this success to other cancers remains an urgent clinical objective. CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) is a gene nomination platform with the potential to direct next-generation cell product development, but genome-wide surveys using this technology in primary T cells have been limited by prohibitive cell requirements and short-lived activity. Here, we describe a CAR-restricted T cell expansion platform generating yields of CRISPRa-CAR T cells far exceeding those required for genome-scale screening (∼109). CRISPRa activity is sustained by incorporating divergent, duplicate elongation factor 1α core/human T cell leukemia virus hybrid promoters and by delivering guide RNAs late by lentiviral transduction to avoid losing perturbations that compromise early T cell activation or expansion. Manufactured CRISPRa-CAR T cells maintain potent on-target gene overexpression (>85% target+) across varied cell subsets, including those associated with T cell exhaustion, and over extended culture periods. When applied to survival-based genome-wide screens, CRISPRa-CAR T cell pools nominate endogenous genes that enhance CAR T cell persistence across varied cytokine levels in the presence of tumor (e.g., IRF4, GFI1, and GSE1). In a proof-of-concept study, we find that the survival effect of GSE1 can be preserved using a clinically relevant transgene overexpression strategy. More broadly, this screening framework establishes a foundation for systematic identification and downstream validation of genes that enhance cellular therapies.

abstract: Screening for high-risk human papillomavirus (HR-HPV) is a pivotal strategy for the prevention of invasive cervical cancer, particularly in resource-constrained settings. In this study, we developed a CRISPR-based compact automated real-time detection system, termed Ccard, for rapid testing of HPV16, HPV18, and the internal reference gene GAPDH through a streamlined workflow. A simple room-temperature treatment efficiently releases nucleic acids directly from swab samples, bypassing the need for extraction. The mixture was driven through the channels and loaded into the reaction chambers on the microfluidic chip by a vacuum pump. The lyophilized reagents in the reaction zone of the microfluidic chip were redissolved. The system subsequently performs a single-step RPA-CRISPR/Cas13a reaction, with real-time detection enabled by an Internet of Things device. The assay achieved detection within 30 min, with a limit of detection (LOD) of 5 copies/µL for both HPV16 and HPV18. Validation with clinical samples demonstrated high sensitivity (96.8% for HPV16 and 100% for HPV18) and 100% specificity. These results highlight the reliability, precision, and strong potential of the Ccard system for rapid testing of HR-HPVs.

abstract: Safe, efficient gene delivery throughout the CNS remains a central obstacle to treating genetic diseases of the brain and spinal cord. We describe BI-TfR1 CapX, a human transferrin receptor (TfR1)-binding AAV capsid that, after a low intravenous dose in adult humanized TFRC mice, transduced more than 80% of cortical and spinal neurons and ∼60% of cortical astrocytes, with reduced distribution and expression in several peripheral tissues relative to AAV9. Unlike other engineered BBB-crossing capsids, CapX bound the CNS vasculature within minutes and a large fraction of its genomes reached parenchymal nuclei within 24 hours. Delivering a Prnp -targeted epigenetic silencer ( Prnp -CHARM), CapX reduced brain Prnp mRNA by over 95% requiring 18-fold fewer vector genomes per brain cell than AAV-PHP.eB for 50% lowering. A CapX delivered dual-vector cytosine base editor installed a protein-truncating PRNP stop codon lowering brain prion protein by 80%. These properties make CapX an attractive vehicle for human CNS gene therapy.

abstract:
UNLABELLED: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infects 90% of the population worldwide and is associated with multiple malignancies, including Burkitt, Hodgkin and post-transplant lymphomas, nasopharyngeal and gastric carcinoma. EBV also triggers autoimmune diseases, including multiple sclerosis and systemic lupus erythematosus. While host factors important for EBV B-cell entry have been defined, including CD21/CR2, MHC class II and R9AP, much remains to be learned about host factors that support post-entry steps of EBV infection. To gain insight, we conducted a human genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen. In addition to known EBV B cell receptors/co-receptors, we identified multiple new factors and pathways essential for EBV B cell infection. These included multiple B cell signaling pathways, actin cytoskeleton and nuclear import factors. Knockout of CD19, its tetraspanin chaperone CD81 or karyopherin subunit alpha 1 (KPNA1, also called importin-α5) significantly impaired establishment of EBV infection. EBV and CD19 co-localized at early stages of EBV infection, and the CD19 cytoplasmic tail was important for EBV infection, suggesting CD19 signaling supports EBV uptake. Depletion of KPNA1 significantly impaired establishment of EBV infection, but did not impair production of infectious EBV upon reactivation of latently infected B cells. Together, these results provide insights into pathways that support EBV B cell infection and identify potential therapeutic targets.
IMPORTANCE: EBV infects ∼90% of humans and causes multiple cancers (Burkitt, Hodgkin, post-transplant lymphomas, nasopharyngeal and gastric carcinoma) and autoimmune diseases (MS, lupus). Yet while B cell entry receptors (CD21/CR2, MHC-II, R9AP) were known, the host machinery needed after entry - for the virus to actually establish infection was largely uncharacterized. This study fills that gap. Using CRISPR-Cas9 screening across the whole genome (rather than testing candidate genes), the study uncovered entire pathways B-cell signaling, actin cytoskeleton remodeling, and nuclear import as essential for infection, expanding the known host-dependency landscape well beyond entry receptors. Because these are discrete, druggable host factors tied to a specific stage of infection (establishment, not maintenance or reactivation), they represent candidate targets for preventing EBV-driven malignancies and autoimmune disease potentially more tractable than targeting the virus itself. The work moves EBV research beyond entry receptors to define the post-entry host dependencies that let the virus successfully infect B cells, identifying CD19 signaling and KPNA1-mediated nuclear import as new, targetable choke points relevant to EBV-associated cancers and autoimmunity.

abstract:
UNLABELLED: Impaired fracture healing remains a significant clinical challenge. Bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) and the exosomes (BMSC-Exos) play a pivotal role in bone regeneration, partly by transferring functional microRNAs (miRNAs). A-to-I RNA editing can profoundly alter miRNA function, but its role in fracture healing, particularly for miRNA-99a-5p, is underexplored. We first profiled differentially edited miRNAs in serum from 50 fracture patients and healthy controls. A murine fracture model was established and treated with BMSC-Exos, where either the edited or wild-type form of miRNA-99a-5p was knocked down. In vitro studies involved transfecting BMSCs with ADAR expression vectors to investigate editing mechanisms, and overexpressing/inhibiting edited/wild-type miRNA-99a-5p in MC3T3-E1C osteoblasts to elucidate its direct functional impacts on osteogenic differentiation, apoptosis, proliferation, and migration. Validation of target genes were performed by dual-luciferase reporter assays, qPCR, and Western blot. Key readouts included alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity, Alizarin Red S (ARS) staining, flow cytometry, Transwell migration, CCK-8 proliferation assays and HE staining. Clinical analysis revealed significantly lower A-to-I edited miRNA-99a-5p levels in fracture patients, correlating with delayed union. In mice, BMSC-Exos promoted fracture healing, an effect attenuated by edited miRNA-99a-5p knockdown. In vitro, edited miRNA-99a-5p enhanced osteogenesis and inhibited apoptosis, while the wild-type form had opposing effects. ADAR2 mediated this editing. Edited miRNA-99a-5p directly targeted and suppressed Growth Differentiation Factor 11 (GDF11) expression. Importantly, GDF11 overexpression reversed the pro-osteogenic effects of edited miRNA-99a-5p, in both direct and exosome-mediated contexts. Reduced A-to-I editing of miRNA-99a-5p is associated with impaired fracture healing. BMSC-Exos facilitate bone repair by delivering ADAR2-edited miRNA-99a-5p, which promotes osteogenic differentiation and bone formation through the specific targeting and downregulation of GDF11. This study uncovers a novel exosome-mediated RNA editing pathway critical for fracture healing and highlights edited miRNA-99a-5p and GDF11 as potential therapeutic targets for bone repair.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s10616-026-01080-x.

abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic immune-mediated skin disorder characterized by persistent inflammation, epidermal hyperproliferation, and complex interactions among immune cells, keratinocytes, cytokines, and genetic factors. Although conventional topical agents, systemic small molecules, and biologics have improved disease management, their clinical utility is often limited by insufficient efficacy, adverse effects, treatment resistance, and poor patient adherence. Recent advances in molecular biology have identified numerous pathogenic genes, signaling pathways, and regulatory RNAs involved in psoriasis, providing opportunities for the development of gene-based therapeutics, including antisense oligonucleotides, plasmid DNAs, small interfering RNAs, messenger RNAs, microRNAs, aptamers, and CRISPR/Cas9 systems. These therapeutics enable precise modulation of disease-associated targets at the genomic and transcriptional levels, offering advantages over conventional pharmacological approaches. However, their topical administration is hindered by the formidable cutaneous barrier, limited skin penetration, poor cellular uptake, and susceptibility to enzymatic degradation. This review summarizes the cellular, molecular, and genetic mechanisms underlying psoriasis pathogenesis and discusses the therapeutic potential of diverse gene-based approaches. Particular emphasis is placed on topical delivery platforms designed to overcome cutaneous barriers, including permeation enhancers, nanocarrier-based systems, and physical enhancement technologies. Recent advances in the integration of these delivery strategies with gene therapeutics for targeted psoriasis treatment are highlighted. Finally, current challenges related to delivery efficiency, long-term safety, manufacturing scalability, and regulatory approval are discussed, together with future perspectives for the clinical translation of topical gene-based therapeutics toward precision psoriasis management.

abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the deadliest malignancies. Dysregulated RNA splicing has emerged as a critical mechanism contributing to PDAC progression. However, whether structural components of the spliceosome regulate oncogenic alternative splicing was not known. Here, we identify the nineteen complex (NTC) component BCAS2/SPF27 as a critical regulator of PDAC progression. Elevated expression of BCAS2 in PDAC is associated with poor patient outcomes. Transcriptomic analyses revealed that BCAS2 specifically regulates alternative exons with weak splice sites. In particular, BCAS2 promotes SOS1 exon 21 inclusion and consequently RAC-signaling activation. Furthermore, splice-switching antisense oligonucleotide (ASO)-mediated skipping of SOS1 exon 21 suppressed PDAC proliferation and migration. Our findings uncover a role of BCAS2 in the regulation of weak splice-site usage and identify the BCAS2-SOS1-RAC signaling axis as a potential therapeutic vulnerability in pancreatic cancer.

abstract: Therapeutic siRNAs are a major clinical modality for hepatic gene silencing, but efficient extrahepatic delivery and multi-gene modulation remain significant barriers. Nucleic acid nanotechnology offers programmable assembly, but conventional structures suffer from enzymatic instability in vivo . Here we report fully chemically modified RNA nanostructures (FMRNs)-a vehicle-free platform entirely composed of stabilized therapeutic nucleic acids that integrate structural precision with metabolic durability. Following systemic administration, FMRNs exhibit enhanced pharmacokinetics and extrahepatic accumulation, with in vivo behavior influenced greatly by hydrodynamic size rather than molecular weight. Using triangular and square geometries, we demonstrate programmable control over siRNA stoichiometry to achieve sustained, simultaneous silencing of up to four genes from a single entity. Nanostructure assembly alone drives productive delivery, especially to heart and muscle, matching lipophilic conjugation. Furthermore, cerebrospinal fluid administration reveals that larger FMRNs improve central nervous system distribution and retention revealing physicochemical parameters that impact brain exposure. FMRNs establish a modular and effective platform combining improved pharmacokinetics, extrahepatic delivery, and multi-gene silencing for complex diseases.

abstract: The recent CRISPR-Cas12b gene editing system, which recognizes DNA targets based on reprogrammed RNA, is increasingly being utilized in various fields. We developed an advanced base-editing technology that seamlessly integrates the TadA8e deaminase with an inactivated dBhCas12b (dead Bacillus hisashii Cas12b) module, enabling precise single-base DNA substitutions in human cell lines. Using the TadA8e-dBhCas12b module, we successfully induced single-base (A-to-G) substitutions at genomic target sites in HEK293FT cells, with an efficiency ranging from 3.96% ± 1.10%-25.78% ± 0.78%, with minimal unintended indel formation due to target DNA nicking. Notably, the editing window of the TadA8e-dBhCas12b module, spanning approximately positions 5-10, can be precisely modulated through the introduction of point mutations within the RuvC domain and the fusion of nonspecific DNA-binding domains, such as Sso7d. These modifications enable efficient base editing at target sites containing thymine-rich protospacer-adjacent motifs (PAMs). The optimized TadA8e-dBhCas12b platform therefore represents a complementary alternative to conventional CRISPR-Cas9-derived base editors and may broaden the range of targetable pathogenic variants, particularly those located within T-rich genomic contexts. Its DNA context-dependent editing window and expanded targeting capacity highlight its potential utility in both basic biological research and therapeutic genome editing.

abstract: Marburg virus disease (MVD), a deadly zoonotic illness in humans, is caused by the Marburg virus (MARV), a single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the Orthomarburgvirus genus of the Filoviridae family. There are currently no approved vaccines or efficient antiviral therapies for MARV, despite high morbidity and fatality rates of the virus, particularly in Africa. Recognizing its epidemic potential and its inclusion on the WHO list of blueprint priority pathogens, an immunoinformatics approach was used to design novel multi-epitope saRNA vaccine candidates (MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII) targeting the viral GP, NP, VP40, and VP35 via CD8 + , CD4 + , and B cell epitopes. These epitopes were derived from target protein sequences and incorporated into MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII after validation for antigenicity, non-allergenicity, non-toxicity, and conservation. Additionally, the selected epitopes were conjugated to suitable adjuvants via various linkers, thereby enabling the design of a potentially stable vaccine. Additionally, the designed MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII were incorporated into the standard saRNA model, in which ORF-2 encodes the target vaccine peptide. Moreover, biophysical analyses unveiled that the developed vaccines are basic (pI < 7), soluble (GRAVY < 0), and stable (aliphatic index < 80). Subsequently, docking of MB-saVaxI to TLR2 (-938.3) and TLR4 (-902.4), and MB-saVaxII to TLR3 (-1485.4) and TLR7 (-1543.6) demonstrated significant affinity, with detailed hydrogen-bond interactions validated by MM-GBSA and molecular dynamics simulations. Furthermore, MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII were effectively cloned in-silico into Escherichia coli, and immune simulations indicated that the vaccines triggered robust innate and adaptive immunity, with a sustained memory response and TH cell activation, as evidenced by IFN-γ and IL-2 production. Additionally, the mRNA structure of MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII remained stable throughout the expression pathway in the host. However, extensive in-vitro and in-vivo studies are needed to establish the safety and efficacy of this vaccine candidate conclusively.

title: Immunoinformatics and reverse vaccinology design of self-amplifying RNA vaccine against marburg virus with structural dynamics and immune simulation analysis.

abstract: Therapeutic mRNA vaccines are a clinically validated cancer immunotherapy platform using in vitro transcribed mRNA encoding tumor antigens to induce durable anti-tumor immunity. Advances in mRNA engineering, lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery, and immunomodulatory combinations have propelled this approach from preclinical models to randomized trials with survival benefit. This review systematically examines vaccine efficacy through an antigen-delivery-immunomodulation tripartite framework. We trace the evolution from shared tumor-associated antigens to personalized neoantigens identified by computational pipelines, discuss ionizable lipid chemistry and LNP formulation for controlled tissue tropism and transfection, and analyze the bidirectional crosstalk between vaccine components and innate immune sensing that shapes adaptive T cell responses. Clinical evidence across melanoma, pancreatic cancer, non-small cell lung cancer, and other solid tumors is critically evaluated, alongside combination strategies-checkpoint blockade, oncolytic virotherapy, and adoptive cell therapy to overcome TME resistance. Persistent challenges include optimal neoantigen selection, standardized immune monitoring, and predictive biomarkers. We conclude that future research should prioritize systematic optimization of the tripartite design through multi-antigen targeting, tissue-specific delivery engineering, and rational combination immunotherapy, aiming to establish mRNA cancer vaccines as a standard-of-care modality.
