abstract: This Phase 1 study will evaluate the safety, tolerability, and immune responses of investigational CH505 HIV vaccine regimens in adults in overall good health without HIV. Participants will receive CH505 protein nanoparticle vaccines (DV901-NP) formulated with the investigational adjuvant ACU-026-001-1, followed by either CH505 protein nanoparticle (DV902-NP) or CH505 mRNA vaccine boosters. The study will assess the ability of these regimens to induce HIV-specific immune responses, including B-cell responses associated with the development of broadly neutralizing antibodies. An immunology cohort will also evaluate how the location of booster vaccination affects immune responses.

abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has achieved remarkable remission rates exceeding 80% in relapsed/refractory pediatric B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL), yet 40-50% of patients eventually relapse within the first year. This therapeutic ceiling is not a single failure mode but the convergence of at least four interrelated layers: loss of CAR-T persistence, antigen escape driven by CD19 splicing variants and lineage switch, CAR-T cell-intrinsic exhaustion from chronic tonic signaling, and an immunosuppressive bone marrow microenvironment that actively extinguishes effector function. Our systematic analysis of 226 pediatric-eligible CAR-T trials shows that 95.6% are Phase I-II, 3.5% (8/226) are registered as Phase III/IV, and 58 of 102 completed trials (56.9%) had no outcome recorded in the source database. In this Perspective, we synthesize the molecular mechanisms of CAR-T resistance, contextualize them within the current clinical trial landscape, and critically evaluate emerging engineering strategies-from dual-targeting and armored CAR architectures to CRISPR-edited allogeneic products and in vivo mRNA delivery. We argue that progress depends on both smarter receptor design and structural reforms in trial design, outcome transparency and global collaboration.

abstract: Patient-derived tumor organoids (PDOs) closely preserve the cellular heterogeneity, histopathology, and molecular features of the original tumors, making them powerful preclinical models. Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) are an emerging class of precision medicines that modulate gene expression at the RNA level with high target specificity, yet their application in organoid systems remains underexplored. Here, we adapted previously described protocols to establish a biobank of prostate cancer (PC) PDOs, achieving a high initial growth success rate (>90%). Histological and molecular analyses confirmed the preservation of key tumor features. Using these models, we assessed several ASOs, with particular emphasis on OGX-427 (Apatorsen), an ASO targeting heat shock protein 27 (HSP27) that has been evaluated in phase I/II clinical trials. While OGX-427 effectively suppressed HSP27 expression and inhibited cell growth in 2D cultures, its efficacy was markedly limited in 3D organoids, likely due to extracellular matrix and structural barriers. Removing Matrigel and applying single-cell transfection overcame these barriers, achieving efficient ASO uptake, significant target protein downregulation, and robust, dose-dependent inhibition of organoid growth. These findings underscore the utility of PDOs for evaluating ASO-based therapies and their potential to accelerate precision oncology strategies for PC and other malignancies.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Small interfering RNA (siRNA) has progressed from an experimental gene-silencing tool to an established therapeutic modality through advances in chemical modification and delivery. Lipid nanoparticles (LNP) and N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc)-siRNA conjugates have driven this clinical translation, particularly for liver-directed applications. Extending comparable delivery efficiency and selectivity to non-hepatocyte cell populations and extrahepatic tissues remains a major challenge.
AREAS COVERED: This review examines approved and late-stage siRNA therapeutics and the delivery principles underlying their clinical development. Relevant publications and clinical trial records from 1998 to 2026 were identified through PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov, supplemented by regulatory agency reports. LNP-based delivery, GalNAc-mediated hepatocyte targeting, and emerging strategies for non-parenchymal liver cells and extrahepatic tissues are discussed, with emphasis on the factors governing cell-selective and productive delivery. Next-generation delivery technologies and the therapeutic distinctions between siRNA and antisense oligonucleotides are also considered.
EXPERT OPINION: The next phase of siRNA therapeutics will require a transition from organ-level accumulation toward functional cell-selective delivery. Improved receptor targeting, intracellular trafficking, and endosomal escape, together with rationally designed delivery systems, may extend RNA interference beyond hepatocytes and broaden its therapeutic applications in inflammatory, fibrotic, metabolic, and malignant diseases.

title: siRNA therapeutics: from hepatic delivery to extrahepatic targeting.

abstract: Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) are potent therapeutics that enable precise RNA modulation. However, efficient delivery to tissues and cell types remains a major challenge. Multimerization, linking multiple ASOs to form large constructs, represents a promising strategy to explore delivery and pharmacokinetics modulation. In this study, we utilized an engineered peptide scaffold to synthesize and evaluate multimeric ASOs, with up to four ASOs connected, with or without a delivery ligand (palmitic acid, bicycle-TfR1, or GalNAc). We demonstrate that ASO multimerization does not impair target annealing, ligand binding, or silencing activity but displays endosomal entrapment in vitro, requiring nanoparticle delivery. Using a luciferase reporter assay, we further assessed the strategy's potential for splice-switching oligonucleotides by designing chimeric constructs capable of targeting two splicing sites at once. Our findings establish the synthetic feasibility of the multimers, identify endosomal entrapment as a key in vitro limitation, and outline considerations for future in vivo evaluation.

title: In Vitro Exploration of Antisense and Splice-Switching Oligonucleotide Multimers Using an Engineered Peptide Scaffold.

abstract: Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is a lethal malignant tumor worldwide. Although ferroptosis offers a promising route for curcumin-mediated non-small-cell lung cancer therapy, its efficacy is often constrained by the robust antioxidant defense maintained by the SLC7A11/GSH/GPX4 axis, which continuously sustains cystine uptake, glutathione biosynthesis, and GPX4-dependent lipid peroxide detoxification, thereby maintaining cellular homeostasis. Herein, we developed a glutathione-responsive metal-organic framework nanoplatform for the co-delivery of curcumin and a GPX4-targeting antisense oligonucleotide (ASO). After cellular internalization, the disulfide-bearing framework underwent GSH-triggered disassembly, enabling synchronized release of curcumin and ASO while depleting the intracellular GSH. Released curcumin increased ROS accumulation and disturbed redox homeostasis, whereas ASO silenced GPX4 expression to concurrently disable the antioxidant defense. Flow cytometry and Western blot assays confirmed significant ROS accumulation and SLC7A11 downregulation, which were detailed by molecular dynamics simulations with putative binding modes. Furthermore, the nanocomposite demonstrated robust anticancer effects in 3D multicellular tumor spheroids with a promoted oxidative imbalance. Taken together, this coordinated intervention disrupted the SLC7A11/GSH/GPX4 antioxidant axis, amplified lipid peroxidation, impaired mitochondrial function, and ultimately enhanced ferroptotic vulnerability.

title: Glutathione-Driven Redox Inducer with Disruption of the SLC7A11/GSH/GPX4 Axis for Enhanced Ferroptotic Therapy.

abstract: CAI-Vax (Cancer Antigen Individualized Vaccine Design) arranges selected antigens and generates synonymous coding sequences for personalized mRNA vaccine constructs. We evaluated 357 vaccine-candidate peptides from 31 patients across four published cohorts. At the primary cumulative MHCflurry percentile-rank threshold of [≤]2%, HLA-aware search reduced predicted junction-spanning peptide-allele binder occurrences by 3.49 per junction relative to amino-acid-pattern optimization (paired Hodges-Lehmann estimate; nominal 95% interval 2.75-4.48; Holm-adjusted P = 7.45 x 10-). All 31 primary paired differences and the estimated effects in all 16 threshold-by-normalization settings favored HLA-aware search within the MHCflurry model used for optimization. Among 25 patients with an exact solution for the additive search objective, single-start greedy search found the minimum in 5 patients and the best individual heuristic in 16. Selecting each patients best result across all tested heuristics increased this to 19. MHCflurry and NetMHCpan EL identified identical tied best-plan sets in 6 of 31 patients after rescoring six frozen plans per patient. In a retrospective internal analysis, repeat-aware synonymous encoding reduced maximum 10-mer multiplicity in every patient, with mean codon-use-preference losses of 0.0041-0.0055 across cohorts; however, it performed worse than matched random encoding for 6-mers. These findings demonstrate that HLA-guided construct optimization can reduce predicted junctional binding within the optimization model, although the preferred antigen arrangement depends on the prediction model used. Experimental studies are needed to determine the biological and manufacturing relevance of these computational differences.

title: CAI-Vax: Computational Design of Personalized mRNA Cancer Vaccine Constructs After Antigen Selection

abstract: Next-generation sequencing has radically transformed the diagnostic capability of rare neurodevelopmental disorders (RNDDs), yet translating these molecular insights into viable therapeutics remains a hurdle. While gene-directed modalities, specifically viral-mediated supplementation, antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), and CRISPR-based activation or precision editing, offer a means to rescue loss-of-function phenotypes, successful clinical implementation requires moving past the reductive framework of merely increasing the expression of the target gene towards approaches that account for spatial, developmental, and therapeutic windows. This review uses HNRNPU-related rare neurodevelopmental disorder (HNRNPU-RNDD), a condition marked with global developmental delay and refractory epilepsy, as an exemplar to discuss these translational hurdles. We discuss the homeostatic boundaries of this scaffold attachment factor, where unregulated overexpression risks localised cytotoxicity, and altered chromatin dynamics compromise editing safety. Furthermore, we assess how cell-type sensitivity and narrow developmental windows may dictate clinical efficacy. By using HNRNPU-RNDD to critically analyse the challenges of using each therapeutic platform, we hope to inform the creation of gene-directed therapies that aim to treat disorders resulting from structural pleiotropic dosage-sensitive proteins.

title: Challenges in Gene-Directed Therapies for Rare Neurodevelopmental Disorders Using HNRNPU as an Exemplar.

abstract: Nonsense mutations account for approximately 20% of pathogenic variants in inherited retinal diseases (IRDs). With advances in gene therapy, nucleic acid-based nonsense suppression strategies, including suppressor tRNAs, RNA pseudouridylation, and adenosine-to-inosine RNA editing, have demonstrated therapeutic potential in preclinical studies. These next-generation approaches offer substantial opportunities for engineering and optimization, with the potential to enable precise and efficient restoration of full-length functional proteins. In this review, we propose that IRDs represent an attractive group of diseases for the clinical translation of these next-generation therapies owing to their high burden of nonsense mutations and the unique advantages of ocular gene therapy. We further outline key strategies to accelerate clinical translation, spanning therapeutic engineering, preclinical validation, and mutation-guided clinical trial design.

title: Rethinking nonsense suppression therapies in inherited retinal diseases.

abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing has emerged as one of the most promising strategies in precision medicine applied to ophthalmology. Although its initial development focused on inherited retinal diseases, recent advances have increasingly targeted anterior segment disorders, including herpetic keratitis, hereditary corneal dystrophies, and genetically associated glaucoma. The ability to modify specific DNA or RNA sequences enables direct intervention in molecular pathways involved in inflammatory, degenerative, and infectious disease progression. This review summarizes the biological basis of CRISPR-Cas systems and discusses the main preclinical and translational findings related to corneal and glaucomatous diseases. Current limitations, including off-target effects, immunogenicity, and challenges associated with molecular delivery into ocular tissues, are also addressed. Available evidence suggests that CRISPR-Cas9 may significantly transform the future management of multiple anterior segment diseases.

title: Advances in precision medicine for the anterior segment: Therapeutic applications using CRISPR-Cas9.

abstract: Spinocerebellar Ataxia 27B (SCA27B) is a late-onset neurodegenerative disorder caused by a heterozygous pathogenic GAA•TTC repeat expansion in intron 1 of FGF14. Despite being a common genetic cause of adult-onset cerebellar ataxia, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we performed simultaneous reprogramming and CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing to generate four induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) lines and their respective isogenic gene-corrected controls. All lines exhibited normal karyotypes, pluripotency, and trilineage differentiation capacity. These paired iPSC lines provide a valuable platform for investigating the pathomechanism(s) of SCA27B and can be used for screening of potential therapeutic treatments.

abstract: Gene editing enables precise genetic modifications, revolutionizing disease treatment, crop improvement, and biotechnological innovation. VeCas9, a recently identified CRISPR endonuclease from the Veillonella genus, exhibits a broader protospacer adjacent motif recognition range in comparison with the widely used SpCas9 nuclease. However, its working mechanism and potential applications in gene editing still need to be fully characterized. In this work, by integrating VeCas9 into a graphene-molecule-graphene single-molecule junction platform, we carried out label-free, in situ mechanistic studies of VeCas9 function at the single-molecule level with high temporal resolution. Using this setup, we monitored the dynamic interactions between VeCas9, single-guide RNA, and double-stranded DNA in real time, in both stable and transient binding modes. Through temperature-dependent measurements, we determined the kinetic parameters of key steps in the interaction process. Moreover, a series of double-stranded DNA substrates was employed to examine how various sequence mismatches affect the VeCas9 activity, revealing that its sensitivity depends on the position of the mismatch. More importantly, we directly observed VeCas9-mediated R-loop formation and quantified the time scale of single-base expansion events. These single-molecule observations provide mechanistic insights into the Cas9 function and demonstrate the strong potential of high temporal-resolution single-molecule techniques for studying dynamic biological processes.

abstract: Highly efficient lung-selective mRNA delivery is pivotal for advancing mRNA-based targeted therapy. Here, we report bis(phosphoramidate diester)-based ionizable cationic lipids (bpLs) for lung-specific mRNA delivery via a distinct intercellular transport mechanism. A bpL library is synthesized by modular headgroups (Ha), linkers (Lb), and tails (Tc). In vivo screening identifies the formulated bpLH15L2T8/DOPENP as the top lung-selective lipid nanoparticle (LNP) with superior pulmonary mRNA transfection. We elucidate that mononuclear phagocyte-guided cell-to-cell trafficking of bpLH15L2T8/DOPENP contributes to its high efficiency and selectivity of mRNA expression in lung tissue. p53 mRNA (mp53) delivered by bpLH15L2T8/DOPENP restores p53 function in p53-deficient pulmonary metastases and synergizes with immune checkpoint inhibitors to enhance antitumor immunity and inhibit lung metastasis of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). An all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) prodrug-containing bpLNP is further developed for lung-specific codelivery of ATRA and mp53, which effectively suppresses lung metastasis of cancer stem cell-enriched TNBC.

title: Bis(phosphoramidate diester)-Based Ionizable Lipids for Highly Efficient Lung-Selective mRNA Delivery via Intercellular Transport.

abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are the leading platform for RNA delivery, enabling applications ranging from mRNA vaccines to CRISPR therapeutics. Ionizable lipids, such as DLin-MC3-DMA (MC3), play a central role in nucleic acid encapsulation and intracellular delivery, yet the molecular mechanisms governing LNP structure and function remain incompletely understood. The internal organization of LNP cores is highly sensitive to pH and has been described by inverse hexagonal, cubic, and lamellar phases that influence delivery performance. Here, we investigate the pH-dependent structure and dynamics of MC3-containing LNPs using two-dimensional infrared (2D IR) spectroscopy and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Both experiments and simulations reveal pronounced pH-dependent changes in the local environment surrounding the lipid ester linkage. At pH 4, strong electrostatic interactions between RNA and protonated MC3 produce broader spectral features consistent with increased interfacial heterogeneity and hydration. In addition, the frequency fluctuation dynamics exhibit a 46% slowdown in RNA-loaded LNPs relative to empty LNPs. In contrast, increasing the pH from 4 to 8 narrows the ester carbonyl band by ∼10 cm-1 and yields nearly identical dynamics for loaded and empty LNPs, indicating a more homogeneous and less hydrated lipid interface. MD simulations further demonstrate that MC3 protonation modulates RNA binding, interfacial hydration, and lipid packing. Together, these results highlight RNA-lipid electrostatic interactions as an important factor influencing the local environment within LNPs and potentially their pH-dependent behavior, providing molecular-level insights into the rational design of next-generation RNA delivery systems.

abstract: This is a Phase 1, randomized, controlled, dose-ranging clinical trial to assess the safety and immunogenicity of novel influenza A Group 1 and influenza A Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin (HA) vaccine candidates given as intramuscular injections alone and in combination. A total of 60 healthy men and non-pregnant, non-breastfeeding women aged 18 through 59 years will be enrolled in one of 6 study arms. The 6 arms will consist of: 1) Sequential influenza A Group 1 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 (25 µg) followed by cH5/1 (25 µg), 2) Sequential influenza A Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH15/3 (25 µg) followed by cH4/3 (25 µg), 3) Sequential combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 + cH15/3 (25 µg) followed by cH5/1 + cH4/3 (25 µg), 4) A single dose of combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 + cH15/3 (50 µg) followed by placebo, 5) A single dose of combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH5/1 + cH4/3 (50 µg) followed by placebo, 6) Sequential combined influenza A Group 1 and Group 2 mRNA chimeric hemagglutinin: cH8/1 + cH15/3 (50 µg) followed by cH5/1 + cH4/3 (50 µg). The primary objectives are to evaluate safety and immunogenicity: 1) To assess the safety and reactogenicity of one or two doses of monovalent or bivalent Group 1 and 2 study products and 2) To describe the Group 1 and 2 anti-HA stalk IgG antibody responses of one or two doses of monovalent or bivalent Group 1 and 2 study products by ELISA.

abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is characterized by a dense desmoplastic stroma and early metastatic dissemination, both of which contribute to its poor prognosis. While forkhead box protein 3 (FOXP3) is best known as a lineage-defining transcription factor in regulatory T cells (Tregs), its aberrant expression in cancer cell-specific FOXP3 (c-FOXP3) may also support tumor-cell-intrinsic progression. Our findings suggest that high c-FOXP3 expression is closely linked to aggressive disease behavior and metastatic progression in PDAC. c-FOXP3 enhanced migration, invasion within three-dimensional collagen-rich matrices, and dissemination in orthotopic models. Integrated transcriptomic analysis, chromatin immunoprecipitation, and wild-type versus binding-site-mutant promoter assays identified matrix metalloproteinase 19 (MMP19) as a direct transcriptional target of c-FOXP3. MMP19 silencing significantly attenuated c-FOXP3-driven migration, matrix invasion, and metastasis. Single-cell sequencing further showed that MMP19 is abundant in cancer-associated fibroblasts but also defines a distinct epithelial pool that is reduced after epithelial Foxp3 deletion. Pharmacological profiling did not identify a validated MMP19-selective inhibitor, whereas the FOXP3-targeting antisense oligonucleotide AZD8701 reduced FOXP3 together with MMP19 mRNA and was accompanied by lower PDAC-cell migration and invasion in vitro. Together, these findings extend the known functions of FOXP3 beyond its classical role in immune tolerance and define a tumor-cell-intrinsic c-FOXP3-MMP19 program that supports matrix-invasive behavior in PDAC and provide preliminary evidence that c-FOXP3 is pharmacologically accessible.

title: Cancer cell-specific FOXP3 licenses MMP19-dependent matrix remodeling and metastatic dissemination in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

abstract: This study presents the mitogenome characteristics analysis of Onobrychis viciifolia, including anatomization of repeat sequences, RNA editing site prediction, substitution rate estimation, and phylogenetic and collinearity analyses. Onobrychis viciifolia is a perennial forage legume with high crude protein content. Although its chloroplast genome has been characterized, the mitochondrial genome (mitogenome) had not previously been annotated. In this study, we assembled the first complete mitogenome of O. viciifolia using a hybrid approach, integrating Illumina NovaSeq short-read and Nanopore PromethION long-read data. The single master circular mitogenome spans 351,303 bp (GC content: 45.17%) and encodes 31 protein-coding genes (PCGs), 20 transfer RNAs, and 4 ribosomal RNAs. Through structural analysis, we identified 76 simple sequence repeats, 144 dispersed repeats, and 6 tandem repeats. Codon usage analysis of 9533 codons revealed a pronounced bias for TTA-encoded leucine (relative synonymous codon usage = 1.53). The analysis of synonymous (Ks) and nonsynonymous (Ka) substitution rates (Ka/Ks) of 21 core genes from 20 legume species revealed that the majority of genes were subject to purifying selection, whereas potential positive selection signals were detected in the ccmB and nad9 genes. We predicted 459 RNA editing sites, with nad4 and ccmB exhibiting higher editing frequencies of 45 and 34 events, respectively. Comparative mitogenomic analysis detected 37 chloroplast-derived sequences (total length: 11,539 bp; 3.28% of the mitogenome), including four transfer RNA genes (trnD-GUC, trnH-GUG, trnM-CAU, and trnF-GAA). Phylogenetic analysis indicated that O. viciifolia and Astragalus complanatus are most closely related, with the node supported by a bootstrap value of 100%, which was corroborated by the phylogenetic tree constructed from 23 plant species. Collinearity analysis further revealed the highly rearranged nature of its mitochondrial genome structure. The assembled and annotated mitogenome provides a valuable resource for investigating cytoplasmic inheritance mechanisms.

abstract: Argonaute (Ago) proteins play pivotal roles in nucleic acid targeting across eukaryotes and prokaryotes. While eukaryotic Ago (eAgo) proteins utilize RNA guides to cleave complementary RNA, prokaryotic Ago (pAgo) proteins often employ DNA guides for DNA targeting. This study focuses on the short pAgo system from Pleomorphomonas koreensis (Pko-SPARDA), which consists of a DUF4365-APAZ protein (PkoRE) and an Ago protein (PkoAgo). Upon RNA-guided target DNA recognition, Pko-SPARDA exhibits nonspecific cleavage activity toward ssDNA, dsDNA, and RNA, demonstrating potential for nucleic acid detection. Biochemical characterization revealed that Pko-SPARDA prefers Mn2+ or Mg2+ as cofactors, operates optimally at 40-45 °C, and is sensitive to mismatches in the central and 3'-supplementary regions of the guide RNA. Notably, the system accommodates a range of guide lengths (14-40 nt) and shows higher activity with 5'-phosphorylated guides. Additionally, guide RNA 5'-phosphorylation universally enhances Pko-SPARDA trans-cleavage activity, and this principle extends to microRNA-guided activation, advancing the understanding of short pAgos and highlighting Pko-SPARDA's utility in molecular diagnostics by bridging a gap left by CRISPR systems due to its lack of sequence constraints like PAM motifs.

abstract: Somatosensation is mediated by dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons, which convert physical and chemical stimuli into electrical signals. However, the full repertoire of molecular components underlying somatosensation remains incompletely identified. Here we developed an efficient postnatal CRISPR-Cas9 knockout platform for interrogating DRG-expressed genes (such as Piezo2, Trpv1 and Scn9a) in mice using AAV9-mediated single-guide RNA delivery. Combining this approach with somatosensory behavioral assays, we performed a targeted screen of 20 genes and identified Creld1 as a cross-model regulator of somatosensation. Either single-guide RNA-mediated postnatal knockout or tamoxifen-induced Cre-mediated deletion of Creld1 in DRG neurons resulted in profound behavioral deficits in touch, temperature, pain and itch, whereas its overexpression enhanced touch and thermal responses. Mechanistically, CRELD1 functions as an auxiliary regulator of voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav) for controlling DRG neuron excitability. Together, this work establishes a robust postnatal screening platform for behavioral genomics and identifies Creld1 as a master regulator of somatosensory function.
